Before the orders of the day are called, I would like to ask a further question of my right hon. friend in respect of the Colonial Imperial Conference. 1 have had occasion since yesterday to look over the precis of the proceedings alluded to by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) and would like to ask if this document, which the government intends communicating to the House, is the report of the proceedings of the Imperial Conference, or whether there is something more to lay before the House in connection with the conference, and if so when it will be laid before the House?
Right hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister). The document which is in the hands of my hon. friend is the precis, so far as I have been able to judge, of the proceedings of the conference, which was issued from day to day to the press, and which has been put in pamphlet form.
At the opening of the conference, a motion was made that the press should be admitted to the proceedings. This motion * was not carried. It was determined at this conference, as at the last, that a precis of the proceedings should be issued from day to day to the press, and this was done accordingly. So far as I have been able to judge, this precis, which has been issued from day to day, has been issued in published form and put upon the table of parliament, but that is not the official document which contains a verbatim report of the whole proceedings of the conference, and which is the document intended to be communicated to the public.
I think this must be an official document inasmuch as it has been presented to parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is, but my hon. friend will understand that the dis-cussions_ were not given verbatim in the precis. This precis was prepared by an officer of the Colonial Department, I think, Mr. Hughes. That was given to the press, but it would not be satisfactory to my hon. friend. What the public wants to know is everything that took place, as was suggested by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) yesterday. That is the document which it is intended to lay before parliament.
Might I ask how soon my right hon. friend expects the House will be in possession of the document?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no more information than my hon.-friend upon this subject, but I should expect it from day to day.

I proposed to th© Minister of Labour that he should appoint a commission similar to the Railway Commission, before whom parties could be heard, and that when that commission gives its award it would be binding upon the parties, and it would be illegal to have any strike or lock-out.

The hon. minister made that statement yesterday, and I would now repeat that I never made a suggestion to him with reference to that matter verbally in my life. I wrote to him, and he has my letter and I challenge him to pro-

duce it, and if it be in accord with the statement he made here to the House, then I am willing to acknowledge the corn. But until he produces that letter and proves his statement, he must lie under the charge of having made a statement in this House which is not in accord with the facts, and be branded, as he should be, with trying by misrepresentation to injure a political opponent. I wrote to the hon. minister that I had gone out and visited the coal mines where the strike was, and after conversation with the mine owners and with the men, I wrote the hon. minister and suggested a plan, and he wrote back thanking me for the suggestion, and saying that he would consider it. My suggestion was that the government should appoint a permanent commission, similar to the railway commission, to which employers and employees could appeal if they had grievances.
If the men had a grievance in reference to not getting sufficient pay or anything of that kind, they could make a complaint to the commission and the commission would hear them. The employers would have a similar right, and it should be unlawful for the men to strike.. If a man wanted to leave his employment he had a perfect right to do so, but no right to prevent another man from taking his place. This was- my suggestion. Why, therefore, should the minister get up here and say to the House that I wanted the government to drive the men back to work at the point of the bayonet? I say that a minister who would make a statement of that kind, which is not correct, is not qualified for the position he holds. And if the Prime Minister finds that a minister would make statements which are not true, he should expel him from the government immediately. '
Sir WILFRID LAURIElt. Order.

The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) may call ' order,' but until he reprimands his Minister of Labour for making a statement such as I have quoted I do not think he can call me to order. Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker,
I desire to call attention to a matter which was mentioned two days ago in this House, namely, the Chinese Investigation^ Commission. This commission was appointed last December to take evidence, took evidence from December until March, and presented its report to this government nearly, or over, two months ago with th&. evidence upon which the report is presented. These matters are common property of the public in British Columbia, particularly in Vancouver where the people are greatly con.-cerned as to the outcome of that investigation. It is necessary, if parliament is_ to have any voice, any chance to know during this session what has been the result of that inquiry, that the report should be voluntarily laid on the table by the government without awaiting the ordinary procedure of an order of the House for its production. I had thought that the report would have come in ordinary course on the reassembling of parliament, judging particularly from the fact, that, two or three weeks before the holidays I inquired about it in the House in conjunction with the Bill to amend the Chinese Immigration Act, suggesting that the report should be brought down before we proceeded with the Bill, and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) m charge of the Bill stated that the request was a very reasonable one, thus signifying the consent of the government to^ produce the report at an early day. Having these facts in mind I asked the other day.
Has the report of Mr. Justice Murphy of the Chinese Investigation Committee at Van-

couver been received, and if so will it be laid on the table without an order of the House?
The answer to this was as follows:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The report has been received by the Department of Trade and Commerce, but in the absence of the minister I am not able to say anything in reference to it except that it is under consideration.
Two days have elapsed since then. It is plain to me that if the government intends to give us the benefit of the information contained in that report -the minister responsible would have taken action before now, but we have no report, and no information as to the report.
To show the gravity of the occasion, I may mention that at the lowest estimate the frauds dealt with by this commission have caused a loss to the revenue of Canada of fully $1,000,000, that they involve a widespread conspiracy extending from Canada across the Pacific to China, and involving not only government officials, but consular officials in China; they involve the Customs Department in opium smuggling, and other smuggling frauds as well as those in relation to Chinese immigration. The circumstances were explained during the course of the trial to several members of this government by persons in a position to know whereof they speak. The ministers to whom they have been explained as shown by the evidence, being the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson), the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright), the Minister of Labour (Mr. King), and the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman). These gentlemen at various times, have been put in possession of the details of these startling frauds as to which it was thought they might show some personal interest. Yet, having appointed a commission, and having received the report of the commission, we find that none of these gentlemen seemingly have had the curiosity to examine the report or determine upon any course of action to be taken with respect to it. That is a position of affairs, which, I submit should not be allowed to continue without protest. And, if I make the protest to-day it is because, in the present perilous condition of this parliament there is no knowing from day to day that further opportunity will be available to place the facts before the public, we must take any opportunity that offers. Now we are entitled, I think, to have that report and the evidence laid upon the table of this House, and placed in the possession of the members. In the absence of the report I have some well authenticated facts which we can present, thanks to the enterprise of the newspapers of Vancouver. We have

some indication of the scope of the inquiry in a letter sent to this government by a person in a very responsible position in Vancouver, selected by them to be a judge of the county court, a man of well known integrity and probity, who wrote during last fall to this effect, and I quote from the evidence as taken in Vancouver:
Judge Grant, who had written to the Minister of Customs suggesting that ' the microbe of graft was evident in the ranks of the Liberal party in this province/ and expressing satisfaction that the inquiry was to take place and also asking that the matter be thoroughly investigated in spite of the social prominence of some of the parties implicated, was on the stand.	! j
The following paragraphs are culled from that letter:
We observe with great satisfaction' the feeling of the Dominion government in deciding to appoint a commission to investigate alleged frauds in connection with the importation of Chinese through this port and Victoria. There is no doubt that there exists a large scheme to defraud the government, and that certain parasites of the Liberal government have profited thereby.
I understand that these same parasites are doing all in their power to prevent the appointment of a commission, but I trust that the government which has done so much in the past to ferret out graft, will see that this also is looked into and that the facts are made public, notwithstanding the high social and party standing of its perpetrators.
The microbe of graft is evident in the Liberal party in this province, and no serum is more effective than the light by way of a searching investigation.
The report proceeds to say:
Judge Grant, in his evidence yesterday said that the allegations he had made in his letter were based on what he had been told hy old members of the Liberal party. He declared that the questions referred to were not only Chinese immigration, but the fishermen's licenses and the Japanese element.
He had been told that a number of men in Nanaimo, who were not bona fide fishermen, apply for licenses and sell them to Vancouver men, who again dispose of them at a considerable profit to the Japanese.
The reference to the attempts to stop the investigation were also based on hearsay, said the witness. He did not propose to disclose the name of his informant.
Mr. Justice Murphy-I must insist that you disclose the name.
But My Lord, I'd rather

Mr. Justice Murphy-As long as I am sitting on this commission I must insist on going into matters fully as they come up. I must insist on hearing his name.
The witness explained that he would prefer to give it privately to the commissioner or the counsel. He had just met the man on the street a few days after the death of Collector Bowell's daughter.
Mr. Judge Murphy-I am very sorry, but I cannot allow the name to be given in private. This is not a star chamber proposition.

There is quite a lot of testimony from the same witness, but the names referred to are not disclosed, so I shall not read further. The report proceeds:

Senkler, K.C., President of the Liberal Association, was the next witness. He said that as chairman of the patronage committee, he had not come in contact with any fraud in connection with Chinese immigration. He admitted that when a vacancy occurred in the Customs Department it had been the custom for the patronage committee to recommend a man. The name was submitted to Ottawa and acted upon. He claimed that Controller -of Customs Bowell had made appointments on his own responsibility of a temporary character.
He said that the patronage system was common throughout the Dominion. He believed that money had been made out of Chinese immigration but claimed not by any members of the Liberal Association.
Here we have a belief stated by a gentleman high in the confidence of this government, a gentleman who has been a candidate of the party in Vancouver, and who now holds the responsible position of president of (the Liberal Association in the great city of Vancouver, who says:
Ho believed that money had been made out of Chinese immigration, but claimed not by any members of the Liberal Association.
During his absence from Vancouver he discovered a telegram had been dispatched to Sir Wilfrid Laurier protesting against the inquiry. Mr. Senkler said on his return he at once informed Sir Wilfrod that the patronage committee had met and wished the inquiry to proceed. He did not know who had sent the telegram or who had signed it.
So we see that this inquiry has been conducted under the most august auspices, that is under the auspices of the patronage committee of the city of Vancouver, whose consent, apparently, had to be obtained before a million dollar fraud could be investigated.
As to this mysterious telegram, I am informed, although I have not under my hand that portion : of the evidence, that it turned out afterwards to have been sent by the secretary of the Liberal Association after a meeting held in the office of the gentleman who repudiated it, and that the secretary of the Liberal Association was in the 'habit of sending official telegrams of this kind attaching thereto the name of the president of the association, so that we may take the gentleman s disclaimer of any knowledge of it as personal only and as not absolving the Liberal association there from the desire first of all to stop a revelation which they feared to have made and their later consent to it as merely forced by the knowledge that , the facts would come out anyhow.
At the risk of taking up valuable time of this House I wish to read from the evidence as reported verbatim in the Vancouver press, some of the most striking passages. I regret that I have not the document itself which is now in the possession of the government, and which I should have, especially because the finding of Mr. Justice Murphy might throw some different light upon what seem to be cloudy passages in the evidence. But since the government refuse to give us this information we must do the best we can with what we have at our disposal.
I have here now the evidence which I said I had not under my hand, as to this mysterious telegram, and I shall read a portion of it. In the 'News-Advertiser' of Vancouver of December 30, I find this:
The patronage committee of the Liberal Association was again ' on the grill ' at the morning session of the commission, when Mr A. M. Pound was exhaustively examined concerning the telegram sent in the name of Mr. Senkler, K.C., chairman of the commission.
Mr. Pound admitted that the draft of the telegram produced was in his own hand-writing, but he did not admit that he saw the actual telegram that was sent to the officials^ of the department at Ottawa. At the request of Mr. G. E. McCrossan, Mr. Justice Murphy agreed to issue an order for the _ telegraph company to produce their file for inspection.
The sending of a telegram on the matter had been discussed at a meeting, said the witness, and the reason they had decided to ask for the reinstatement of Yip On was that the customs officials stated that nothing had been proved against him, and that they had every confidence in him. Asked whether he thought that was a sufficient reason to go to Sir Wilfrid Laurier above Mr. Foster's head, witness replied in the affirmative.
He had no reason for supposing that Mr. Foster, or the department which sent him did not know what they were doing, but the information given was conflicting, caused, he thought, by one tong being against another.
This is the telegram, dated September 23:
Recommend reinstatement Yip On approved
by our friends and customs officials; charges not proved; our friends object to drastic action of O'Hara in suspending collector Bowell.
I was wrong in saying that the meeting was held in the office of the chairman of the Liberal executive. I read here:
Wlio remained in the room of Messrs. Kelly Douglas' office when you left?

Yes, at the time.

'And the sole desire for this,' exclaimed counsel ' was shown in two telegrams-the reinstatement of Yip On and the leaving of the appointment to the patronage committee. Anything else? he satirically concluded.

' When was that? '
It was shortly after the Drummond and Arthabaska election.
It was shortly after the Drummond and Arthabaska election when the fear of God was in the hearts of these Liberals in Vancouver, that they reluctantly consented to an investigation which just before that momentous event they had resolutely set themselves to prevent if they possibly could.
Now, as to the origin of these frauds. As I said, it is no new matter, but this has been going on ever since 1907, shortly after the Chinese Immigration Act was amended by this parliament for no honest purpose that any one has ever been able to discover, but under circumstances which gave ground for protests at that time, and for the assertion that the amendments were made with the sole idea of facilitating the frauds which have occurred. These protests were made locally to my knowledge when the amendments were before the House, and they have been fully borne out by subsequent developments which have shown nothing but fraud to have resulted from the larger scope given for the importation of so-called Chinese merchants and students. I have but little to add to the sordid story, the recital of which occupied the attention of the House this afternoon, but there are still a few passages which I would like to put on record to complete one or two points as to which some difference of opinion was expressed.
When the House rose at six o'clock, I had been reading from the evidence of Mr. Mclnnes at Vancouver, and the proposal to change the system of Chinese immigration to make it -correspond with that respecting the Japanese. Continuing the reading from the '.News-Advertiser,' I find in the issue of January 24th, in the review of Mr. Mclnnes's evidence, the following:

Another statement made by Mr. Mclnnes was that he thought that Canada had blundered in every way in its entire Chinese policy. Code names for about a score of prominent government and local personages were disclosed, and provoked a good deal of merriment amongst thp crowd assembled. I have read from the sworn evidence. I have not gone beyond January 25th yet. I will read the statement from the 'News-Advertiser' again.

In connection with the telegram sent in the name of Mr. J. H. Senkler, K.C., suggesting ' the reinstatement of Yip On, and expressing the objection entertained to the drastic action of Mr. O'Hara in suspending collector Bowell,' the letter of Sir Wilfrid Laurier of October 3rd last stated that the Premier had found there was a very strong prima facie case against the Chinese interpreter, and that he had been properly suspended.

In his letter to the Premier of October 8th, Mr. Senkler stated he thought the executive of the Liberal association were wrong in sending the telegram in his name in his absence. They should, if -they had felt so strongly on the matter as they apparently did, have sent it in the name of the secretary

or vice-president, or acting chairman. However, he personally thought most Chinese were proverbially dishonest, and if it were possible to get an interpreter who was not a Chinese, it would be infinitely preferable.
In the 'Advertiser' of January 26th there is a review of the evidence given by Mr. J.os. Martin, K.C., which is as follows:
Mr. Joseph Martin, K.C., M.P., was the star
witness yesterday. His evidence was not -exactly evidence in regard to the definite prints of the inquiry, but it was a scathing indictment, of ' the graft he believed had permeated every department/
His was a meteoric appearance, and he burst in alike on the commission the Dominion government, the local Libei al executive and Mr. Robert Kelly, its chief, in particular. His charges included the statement that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was primarily to blame, and that the Premier ' could stop it all in five minutes if he wanted to do so / that every department in which the Liberal government spent money or had any control' in British *Columbia went through the local Liberal or .ganization here, over which Mr. Robert Kelly was the head; that Mr. Robert Kelly had the *control of every thing in regard to the government's business and in return supplied Lunds for the government campaigns. These -were two of the statements made by ' fighting Joe' and listened to with absorbing attention by the crowded assembly who were present.
Judge Murphy pointed out that Foster had said twice that Mr. Templeman said to him " Foster, I want you to stop this.' Witness said Foster did-not say that to him, but that be said that Mr. Kelly and Dr. Munroe attempted to stop the matter.
Now, there are reams or evidence in addition to what I have read. The inquiry proceeded in Vancouver and Victoria for some time after January 31, to which the files from which I am reading extend, and -which contains all that I propose to read to the House. I think I have read enough to show that a most appalling condition of affairs has existed in Vancouver during the last four years; that persons in a position to know how the revenue has been defrauded have been making continual and repeated complaints since that time; that they ' have^ gone the round of almost the [DOT]whole cabinet with these complaints; that tio relief appears from any quarter until Mr. O'Hara a deputy minister saw fit, off his own bat, to institute an investigation which inspector Foster is declared by Judge Murphy to have said the Minister of Inland Revenue himself wished to have stopped. But the matter Had gone too far to be stopped. It went on, we are told, largely as the result of the fear inspired by the Drummond and Arthabaska 'election* which showed that it was possible to conceive that a day of reckoning could come. The evidence has been in the possession of the government, some of it since December, and the last of it since April last.

And we wind up with a statement in this House a few days ago that, in the absence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce the matter is under consideration, and the ministers do not know when, if ever, that report will be laid before the House, or whether any action will be taken in connection with it. Now, the whole iri'dict-ment, so far as the smuggling of Chinese [DOT] into Canada is concerned, is against the Department of Trade and Commerce primarily to show its utter inefficiency, and its entire neglect of the business entrusted to it. We are told that a colleague of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is doing his level best within the cabinet to relieve the paralysis by having control of the Chinese transferred from a dead department to a live one. We are told by another employee of the government that the only reason that this is not done is that if you take this from the Trade and Commerce Department there will be nothing left for it. In the face of all that, this House is supposed to be content with the statement that the government will not act except on the initiative of the Trade and Commerce Department. I, for one, am not satisfied with that. I am quite satisfied that those of my constituents who form part of the population of the city of Vancouver are not satisfied, that they are earnestly desirous that the government should take some steps to put an end to the gross scandal prevailing there, and they would call me seriously to account if, in common with other members, I was so derelict in my duty to them as to allow the session to pass without some exposition of the state of affairs there, and a demand that some action shall be taken by the government. I leave it to the judgment of the House whether or not the facts indicate that we should put upon the record the opinion of this House as to the failure of the government to deal with these scandals, and to punish the perpetrators who, for a period of many years, have gone unwhipped of justice.

I thought that some minister of the Crown would give an answer to the very serious ind'ictmetnt brought against the - government or give some explanation of the masterly inactivity which appears to have characterized the government in connection with this affair from first to last. I thought the minister for British Columbia (Mr. Templeman) especially would say something. But he chooses to remain silent. It seems to me that this is an extraordinary situation, and yet it is not so different from those we have had to deal with during the last few years. The government found themselves in this situation because of trouble over which, perhaps, in the first

place, they had no control. But the action which they took in the premises was not calculated to impress the public with the bel'ietf that they were very ^.anxious to punish the wrongdoers or stop the wrongdoing, otherwise we should have had different evidence of it from that which we have to-day. Rumours of wrongdoing, dishonesty, and fraud in connection with Chinese immigration, and government officials was brought to the notice of the government several years ago. It was brought to their notice in the most pointed and, direct way, by letters from their officials, by letters from their friends, by conversations they themselves had with those in whom they ought to have full confidence. But, notwithstanding, they appear to have paid no attention to it, and allowed these frauds to contipue. There was finally sufficient information brought to their notice to induce the government to appoint a Royal Commission to inquire into the matter.
They did appoint that commission, and the inquiry went on. It commenced about' the time of the opening of this session last November. That inquiry was confined to two ports, Vancouver and Victoria, and so was not widespread, and did not require a long time to take the evidence. Now, seven months after its appointment, parliament is anxious to see that report, but we are denied that right although the report has been in the hands of the government for two months. Why are we denied that report? Because the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not here. Because the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who happens to occupy a seat in the Upper Chamber, which has adjourned until August 10, is off enjoying himself at his summer residence and may not put in an appearance until that date or afterwards.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He will be here to-morrow.

Is that not strange conduct on the part of ministers and on the part of the Prime Minister himself? In the absence of the minister of any department one of his colleagues invariably administers his department, and surely it was the duty of the minister so acting to at least make an effort to procure this report for parliament. It is a strange parody on ministerial responsibility and executive duty. It is not what the country and this House demands. This House may at any time collapse from its own unfortunate conduct, and parliament be dissolved, and, in the absence of that report we will have no information to give to the country to enable 4he electorate of Canada to judge of the action of the government In connection
with that transaction. Perhaps a year-after the election that report may be presented to the House.
If the evidence given in the press is at. all reliable an awful state of affairs has been disclosed. We see a minister of the Crown controlled by one of his supporters out there in the Tammany of Vancouver, Mr. Kelly, and an executive or patronage committee, a confidential committee who seem to control the whole-affairs of this government in that great city. It was the duty of the Minister of the Interior to look after immigration, but he has done nothing in this matter. The attention of the Minister of Customs was drawn to these frauds in the smuggling of opium and Chinese into the country, but nothing has been done.. Then we have the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) who belongs to the . city, who knows all these men, and who-has been acting through that committee,, that Tammany ring for years, and has had brought to his attention over and over again the discreditable conduct of this committee. Yet there is no effort to do away with it or to purge the unclpanness of that stable out there. So it goes on, masterly inactivity, unconcern, indifference, dishonesty, culpability, crime, fraud, and everything, all brought home to the government in the plainest possible way if this evidence is reliable, and yet the evidence is kept from the House at the time we ought to have it. The report pf the commissioner was finished early in May, but it has- not been presented. This is not the only case of the kind; we had a similar condition with reference to the Marine Department, and were told that everything was all right there. The government from session to session were urged to make an inquiry, but they were able to sidetrack it in some way. Finally a commission was appointed. They attempted to prevent the carrying out of that investigation, to burke the inquiry after it was begun. The commissioners had not time to cover more than a portion of the ground, but they made a partial report of what they inquired into. That report disclosed the most disgraceful state of affairs that was ever known in the running of a department of the government here in Ottawa.
Then what happened? The ministers of the Crown commenced to abuse the commissioners and the commissioners were indicted before this House because of the report they had presented. They were the-criminals, they were held up before the people because they had honestly endeavoured to do their duty. The government could not absolutely burke that inquiry although they stopped it after the inquiry was partially -made. We had following that another one-the Printing Bureau.

The opposition endeavoured to have an inquiry, but they were not allowed to do so. It was voted down because it was said there was nothing wrong. Everything that had transpired that was wrong had been righted and yet there is only a fraction of what should come out that has been laid before this House to enable the House to judge of the state of affairs in the Printing Bureau. In 'every one of these instances the same tactics were followed by the government. The members of the House were kept in the dark as far as possible. The commissioners were prevented from going on with that inquiry as they should have gone on with it. In the case of the Department of Marine and Fisheries there was a second investigation that disclosed a great deal more wrong-doing than the first one and even that only covered part of the ground. From information in our possession we have reason to believe that there are other departments that are as bad as this, if they were inquired into. The opposition have tried over and over again to get a commission of inquiry with full powers to make an investigation into these departments, but every time it has been voted down upon the declaration of ministers that everything was all right and that there was no need for investigation. This, if it had been brought up in this House, would have been treated in tile same way. But while there was a commission appointed and while it did bring out a lot of valuable information, the House is denied the right to see that information, to read, analyse and sift the evidence and present it to the people of the country, who in all human probability will be shortly called upon to express their verdict at the polls in regard to the conduct of this government during their term of office. We cannot have it. Is that treating the electors of the country right? It is an injustice to this House that should not be tolerated, it is an injustice to the electors that should not be tolerated, and I can only hope that when the dav comes that the people must sit in judgment upon them they will have this case before their minds and that they will mete out even-handed justice to their representatives in this House who have made this effort to prevent this information being given to the House or the country as it should be, so that it can be dealt with in a proper way The hon. Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) said that this thing was under consideration. How long will it remain under consideration before it shall fructify in results? With regard to the efforts made to recognize the veterans of the Fenian raid-fiasco, why, it has been under consideration, for 14 years and there is no indication that they have reached a conclusion yet From time to time we have had that declaration from the Prime Minister, from Mr. SPROULE.	[DOT]
the Minister of Militia and from other members of the government. It is still under consideration. As in this case the Minister of Justice declared that it was under their cons;deration. What does that mean to the House or the people of the country? If we are to judge what it means by what we know of other cases where the same expressions have been used and where we have had time to ascertain what tne results have been we are justified in coming to the conclusion that it was under consideration for the purpose of keeping it from the people, keeping it from this House, keeping it in the dark, rather than for the purpose of bringing it to light. I think it is disgraceful, I think it is discreditable, I think it does not reflect credit upon any member of the present government. It happens that by an accident of life some of the members of this government must be in the Senate, but when the House of Commons desires information and if the Senate is not in session there is the easiest way in the world to have it presented to this House, instead of using the fact that the Senate has adjourned and that the minister is off on his summer holidays as an excuse for refusing to give the House the evidence of that important commission which it ought to have to-night and which it ought to be able to read over carefully and take action upon before the House has probably collapsed and a .new election is held.
Right hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister). Mr. Speaker, I did not rise after my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) had taken his seat for the reason, which I will give him very frankly, that, in my estimation, the speech which he made was not so much for the purpose of obtaining information as for the purpose of killing time and obstructing the business of the House. My hon. friend spoke for a matter of three or four hours, certainly for three hours, and there is no reason at all, if he had been anxious to have the information, why he should not have had the answer which he wanted to have in ten minutes. My hon, friend (Mr. Sproule) has. just taken his seat after having devoted fifteen minutes to the same subject and under such circumstances I owe it to him to give him the answer which he requires. An investigation has been made into the condition of things which prevailed in British Columbia with regard to the administration of the Chinese Act. This investigation was held by a Judge of the Supreme Court, Mr. Justice Murphy. His report was sent to my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) who handed it over to the Department of Justice for the purpose of taking action upon it. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth)
98.17

asked me to look over the report to-day and I had a conference with him. I will give frankly to the House the reason why the report has not been placed upon the table of the House. Mr. Justice Murphy's report is a very voluminous one, containing at least 100 pages of foolscap typewritten matter, if not more. I had no time to read it in its entirety, but I looked into it at the conclusion. The conclusion of the report is that certain parties should be prosecuted. These parties have not been prosecuted because they are not at this moment in the country. Mr. Justice Murphy's second recommendation is that this report should not be made public until the prosecutions have been instituted. I have not had the report in my hands to read it over, but 1 presume that if the report and the evidence were disclosed it would, to some extent, interfere with the administration of justice and with reaching the culprits. Under such circumstances we have to make up our minds either to make the report public and therefore give this advantage to the culprits which Mr. Justice Murphy says should not be given or we will have to keep the report to ourselves and be subjected to the very charitable inference that we have something to conceal. I said a moment ago, that I have not yet had an opportunity of looking at the report. It is my intention to look over it with my hon. friend the Minister of Justice in order to -discuss with him what action should be taken upon the report. Then, we shall make further communication to the House and state whether we shall make the report public or not make it public as we deem best in the public interest.

I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman why the Minister of Justice answered in these words :
The report has been received by the Department of Trade and Commerce, but in the absence of the minister, I am not able to say anything in reference to it except that it is under consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The absence of the Minister of Trade anjl Commerce is not to be interpreted as it has been interpreted by my hon. friend that he is to be absent so long as the Senate is adjourned. The minister is to be in Ottawa to-morrow and it is my purpose to discuss this matter with him.

The Minister of Justice gave the idea that the report was in the Trade and Commerce Department, and that he knew nothing about it, whereas it was in the Justice Department, and he might as well have told the House so.

The First Minister has been so unfair as to say that I have brought this matter up simply
for the purpose of wasting time. I give that statement a most positive contradiction.
You can contradict it if you like.

I do not expect to convince the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot). I brought the matter up in pursuance of my duty to a large number of citizens of Vancouver who are my constituents, and in pursuance of my duty to my constituents generally. I asked for this report on two previous occasions without making any remarks at all. The first time I was promised it and the next time the promise had vanished and I was given no information at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I must give my hon. friend the credit of this disclaimer but I am sorry to say his prolixity gave a different' impression.

The Prime Minister ought to make an apology rather than an insinuation. This matter has been in the public press for months past; the evidence has been taken, and largely printed in the newspapers of the country; a report has been made; parliament re-assembles, and there is not one word from any member of the government with regard to that investigation or report. No explanation is given by the ministry as to why the report of that commission has not been submitted to parliament and the inquiry of my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) is met in an evasive way. As a natural result of that, the evidence published in the, press of the country has been placed in part upon ' Hansard ' as it was the duty of my hon. friend from New Westminster to do in view of the apparent unwillingness of the government to give any information to the House or to the country. When the Prime Minister says that this report is not submitted to ' parliament because its submission might interfere with the course of justice I do not understand what he means. I am bound to say that the Prime Minister has not expressed himself in a manner that would carry conviction on that point in my mind. The inquiry was open to the public, and the evidence was published in the newspapers and it does not seem that there can be anything in the suggestion that the placing of the evidence on the table of the House would give these men information which they have not at present. I do not understand the suggestion of the Prime Minister in that respect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Borden) was not in the House when I stated, that, this morning I had a conference with the Minister of Justice upon the subject. I had not time to read
9S39

the voluminous report, but I read the conclusion wherein Mr. Justice Murphy suggests that certain parties should be prosecuted. I am informed by the Department of Justice that these parties are not in the country. Mr. Justice Murphy also recommends that the report should not be made public previous to these prosecutions. That is why the report has not been tabled. I will see the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Trade and Commerce about it again to-morrow, and we will have to decide then whether we shall bring down the report and give to those who are to be prosecuted an advantage which Mr. Justice Murphy says they should not have, or whether, in order to clear ourselves, we shall act against the recommendation of the commissioner and bring the report down.

I would not for a moment criticise a report made by Mr. Justice Murphy, or any other commissioner, but I am not at present able to appreciate the point he makes. I presume there can be nothing in the report which is not founded upon the evidence which was taken in public, and which every one of the men implicated knows. If the Prime Minister on the day parliament met had stated what he has stated to-night, and left it to the members of the House to press or not press for the report, it would have been better. Instead of that, we have an answer of an evasive character in regard to the report, and my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) in the face of that was in duty bound to extort from the government some explanation of their very extraordinary conduct in connection with this matter. I had not followed this subject very closely in the public press, and to-day I have been absolutely astounded at the evidence which seems to have been given before Mr. Justice Murphy in connection with Chinese immigration. Some of that evidence is of the most shocking character, and I should have thought that any government involved as this government has been, would have felt it its duty at the earliest moment to make an explanation to parliament, if any could be made, as to the extraordinary revelations made. I find it stated-not by Conservatives, but by prominent members of the Liberal party in the province of British Columbia-that there was actually a quarrel among them as to how the plunder from the public treasury should be divided. One would suppose that such evidence would bring from the government a prompt statement that effective measures would be taken immediately not only to end such an intolerable condition of affairs, but to bring to justice those who Sir WILFRID LAURIER
have been plundering the people of Canada for many years past.

Mr. Speaker, the right hon. the Prime Minister has stated that the hon. member for New Westminster was taking up the time of the House, and carrying on this discussion purely for the purpose of wasting the time of this House. To me it seems that the party who is guilty of all this loss of time, if there is any, is the right hon. the Prime Minister himself, because had he earlier in the day made a statement such as he has made now, the discussion might have been curtailed, that is, provided the right hon. gentleman had gone a little farther, and stated to the House that in view of the fact that departments of his government have been so derelict in their duty as to hold this report over for three months in order to enable all those likely to be prosecuted to get out of the country, he would bring down the report at once. In fact, he did not apparently know that some one was to be prosecuted until to-day, nor did the Department of Justice know that the judge who made this report had suggested that some one should be prosecuted. For months that report has been pigeonholed in the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the men guilty of defrauding this country of about $1,000,000 have no doubt been aided by information given to them directly or indirectly to leave this country, and thus avoid any prosecution. This is not the first time that the government has been asked for this report. The hon. member for New Westminster has again and again asked that it be presented to the House. One would have thought that in a matter not only involving a great money loss to this country, but showing thaf~a most flagrant conspiracy existed in Vancouver to defraud this country, and that officers employed by a department of the government were in that conspiracy, the government would have as quickly as possible taken action, and laid the report on the table of the House. Instead of that, they have done nothing, and the guilty men are now out of the country. Certainly there was loss of time there on the part of this government. Under the circumstances there was only one course lor the party on this side of the House to pursue, and that was to place on the records of this House the evidence taken by the commission as disclosed in the newspaper reports, and show as clearly as possible the facts connected with this great Tong war carried on between two factions of the Liberal party in British Columbia in the last few months. The birds have flown, and the fact that the Prime Minister has announced in this House that certain people are to be prosecuted is warning to those peo-

pie who are out of the country that if they return they are liable to be placed under arrest. The cat is out of the bag. So far as future prosecutions are concerned, the report might as well be placed on the table of this House by the Prime Minister to-day or to-morrow as a month or six months from now, and I think he should state that he will place tne report on the table to-morrow. The facts disclosed in that report are to all intents and purposes public property at this moment. In justice to this House and the country, I think the evidence should be placed on the records of this House. The hon. member for New Westminster has placed on the records the evidence up to the beginning of February. As his physical powers are not equal to his quoting the evidence for two or three hours more, I think I am justified in assisting him by proceeding to read the evidence taken at the remaining sittings of that commission in British Columbia. That is the only way in which this House can have the facts before it, and then we shall be able to deal with this question in an intelligent manner. It would be very absurd for us to bring in a motion casting any reflection on the government in this matter before we had all the evidence before us, and I am sure that hon. gentlemen opposite, who are so closely and intently listening to the evidence, will be pleased to read it in ' Hansard ' to-morrow. The Minister of Customs is at the head of the department which has to do with the collection of this tax, and he is the first man who should have taken action against these frauds and rascalities; yet he as the principal watch-dog has been absent during the whole afternoon, when this sordid tale has been told in the House. Let us see how this thing occurred. We know that the law with reference to Chinese immigration was changed in 1907, permitting merchants, students and merchants' sons to come to this country. A vast conspiracy was formed, with its ramifications in China and Canada, by which men in China, on payment of $100, were made partners in firms of merchants there. Some who were cooks or laundrymen were in this way raised to the dignity of merchants, and they received consular certificates from China on which were placed their photographs, and in many cases were given new names.
As	near	as	I can understand	it theywere	met	by a man supposed	to bean agent	of	this government, and hehanded them gold coin to the tune of $150 or $200. Drafts were given on imaginary banking houses, and after they came to Vancouver they were met by the commissioner of customs, who was deluded by the interpreter, the latter pretending to ask a great many questions from these men,	but	it was definitely and	clearly
proved that he did not ask them any questions at all, on the other hand he laughed up his sleeve at what he was supposed to say. He made a long face to the customs house officer there who had charge of this end of the business and looked very wise and these men were passed as merchants. Hundreds of them got through in that way, and before I close to-night I propose to show how many were passed! The strange thing about this is that these men were not passed at Victoria-where they might have been passed-or Prince Rupert or Comox, but at Vancouver. The most peculiar thing in connection with it all is the appearance there of a patronage committee which seems to rule over the destinies of the Liberal party on the coast. That patronage committee has since become divided against itself, a great tong war now rages, their dirty linen is being washed before the public, and the names of ministers have been dragged into the light of notoriety, as we read in the evidence given from time to time in these papers.
But members of the opposition have refrained from making any reference to these questions previously during this session. That was not due to the fact that we were not well aware of what was going on or that we did not watch closely the evidence taken before the commissioners in Victoria Vancouver and elsewhere, but because we felt that the Prime Minister of this country and those who have charge of the treasury matters should realize ' the importance of this question and take prompt action. I am satisfied that it was the duty of the'. Prime Minister the moment the commission was appointed to ask the commissioner to make a report direct to him and give him the result of the investigation, by wire if necessary. In this matter this country has suffered a loss to the extent of at least one million dollars through the dishonesty of public servants -lost apparently through the machinations of the patronage committee who stood in with these Chinamen. In the newspapers on the coast at the time, it was stated that the interpreter who worked the racket got $20 a head on those he put in, and that $100 a head went to somebody higher up in the confidence of this party-some man who had power and patronage to distribute?
That is a very sordid and sad tale. I could quite understand it in connection with any other department but a department collecting revenue. In no other British country can we find anything of the kind in connection with the Customs Department. There have been frauds in connection with contracts, and petty grafting in connection with other departments, but such a thing as this in connection with

a department collecting revenue is unknown.
The strangest feature of the whole matter is the apparent and intense Interest shown by the hon. the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) to help somebody out throughout this whole transaction. The holding of nice dinners at which this was discussed, nice little dinners where, according to the witnesses, nobody got drunk, and at which all these matters were threshed out by the patronage committee -these are the facts that came out in the evidence; and I am sure this House will not be satisfied until the whole of the evidence is laid before it in 'Hansard' to-morrow. The only possible way in which we can get this story before the public and the only way that we can get the facts before the people so that they can pass judgment upon it is to have some of the evidence placed upon 'Hansard'. Therefore I would ask the House to be patient with me while I read portions of the evidence from the 1st of February until the inquiry was closed.
On the 1st of February the investigation was resumed, and two Chinese witnesses were examined. These two men were printers. Apparently they have a paper in Vancouver called the ' Sun Bow,' published by the Chinese Association or a Chinese company. They were in need of printers, and they did not seem to have trouble^ in getting Chinese printers.
Reading from the Vancouver 'News Advertiser' of February 1st, page 5 I find the following evidence given by these printers:
Then two Chinese witnesses who had the appearance of students, who were dressed in Kuropean style, were brought in.
This was before the judge who was taking the evidence:
Then two Chinese witnesses, who had the appearance of students and were dressed in European style, were brought in, and Mr. Mc-Crossan suggested that David Lew or the reporter of a Chinese-not English-paper should translate, but Mr. Taylor objected to Lew. The judge suggested Lew should translate subject to check on the part of someone else, but as Mr. Taylor had no one present the judge decided he would not let the men go before they were examined, as the chances were, if he did so, they .might not see the men again.
Eventually Mr. Cum Tow was telephoned for, and while they were waiting for him the paper oath was administered, Lew, first being sworn in as interpreter for the purpose of administering the oath.
Hon gentlemen will understand what a paper oath is. The name of the Chinaman is written on a piece of paper and the paper is then burnt before him. There is another form of Chinese oath known as the 'chicken oath'. They threatened several Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe).
times to use it in this case, but I do not see any evidence that it was used.
Then each witness, whose names were Yip Dit Chor and Yung Jung Sung wrote his name on a slip of paper which was lit and each witness held it until it burnt itself out, 'telling them beforehand, in Chinese, what the oaths meant and the full signification if perjury was committed.
AsMr. Cum Yow had not arrived at 5.20, the judge directed a message to be sent saying the court was waiting, and Mr. McCrossan unavail-ting.ly tried witnesses in English.
Then David Lew started to interpret the questions, and soon after Mr. Cum Yow came in.
"Yip Dit Chor was a typesetter on a Chinese newspaper.''	[DOT]
You will observe his name 'Yip' shows his clan. He was one of the Yip clan, and the interpreter against whom these charges were made was Yip On. I do not know whether this man Yip was a Liberal or an insurgent Liberal. However his name was Yip Dit Chor. He was a typesetter on a Chinese newspaper, and a fearful undertaking it is to set type on a Chinese journal. If the Min-nistor of Railways (Mr. Graham) were here, he would, as he has been a type setter himself, understand what a lot of trouble it is for a man to set type when he has a font 30 feet long and has to run backwards to pick out each letter- a letter being supposed to represent a word, is it any wonder then, that under the circumstances that there was a scarcity of typesetters in Vancouver. However this man was a typesetter and the report goes to say:
Yip Dit Chor was typesetter on a Chinese newspaper here, and followed the same trade in China. He came to Canada on the Mont-eagle about June, 1907, and did not have the handling of a passport^ He did not know whether he paid head .tax or not. He came with Yung Sing Set. Mr. Cum Yow now entered and checked Lew's singing questions and interpretation.
Witness knew that he himself never paid the poll-tax. He met Yip On at the shed, and' was examined by Mr. Howell, who interrogated him as to age, etc., Yip On interpreting.
Was he asked if he was a merchant?
-He was not asked that in Chinese.
You will observe that the interpreter was supposed to ask him that question.
'Did he describe himself as Mak Sis Wah ?' asked Mr. McCrossan, consulting a passport?
He signed his name as Mak Sis Wah, which was not his right name. It was his photograph which appeared on the passport. He never saw the passport before. He paid nothing for it.
Judge Murphy-And it cost you nothing to come into Canada ?
Witness said it was all paid by the Sun Bow Newspaper Company.
At this point arises a very important thing in connection with the importation of

Chinese, and that is this:. .Peonage is recognized in China, and men come to this country whose way is paid and who for years afterwards remain virtually the slaves of the companies or individuals who import them. Anything that will encourage that system of importing Chinese labour into this country helps in maintaining a great evil and a great wrong to these men. This evil grew to great proportions in the United States, where there were societies that enslaved large classes of Chinese who worked night and day but all of whose wages went to these companies. Here you see, was a man taken charge of by a company in China, shipped to Canada, and a passport given him. Why, he was even given a new name. And he comes into the country and pays no poll tax, I think the case is a clear one.
Did Yip On to knowledge of witness know what work witness was coming here to do?- He did not know Yip On at all at that time.
He came over on the 'Mon t.eagle' in company with Yung Ling Sit, another Chinese newspaper typesetter, who had since died. Yung Jung Sung, who had come to the court with him, was also a typesetter here and in China. They did not come on the same vessel.
Did witness ever go before the Viceroy?- Witness did not know how the certificate was obtained. He did not go for it.
A Chinaman in China is supposed to go before the viceroy and get his certificate signed. This man never appeared before the viceroy. Bo you see the law there was violated.
Who got it for him?-He did not remember the man's name. He was a clerk there. Witness was engaged to come here by Long Shu Hun, representing the ' Sun Bow ' newspaper Company.
Did this Long Shu Hun take him to the Yah Wick Company?
He belonged to what company?
What was their business?-Exporters of general dry goods.
Did he know Yip Yen?-Yes.
Where did he meet him?-He saw him at the Yah Wick Company last on the day he left for the steamer.
Witness said he was examined at the detention shed here by a white officer and that Yip On was there. He did not know the name of the white officer, but hi: was a pretty elderly man.
What did Yip On ask you?-
He did not ask witness much questions, hut asked if he was a merchant, the latter replying that he had come here to go into business. Some one in Hong Kong told him to say that.
What did he pay for the passport?-He did not know.
Had he paid any thing at all?-No.
Was it understood the Sun Bow Company were to pay his poll-tax?

All that was said was ' He give you this paper. You go over there. It will be all right.'
He never saw the Viceroy, or went to the British consul. He got the photograph from the Yah Wick Company and travelled as ' Lee Su Hung/ which was not his right name, hut was the name he was told by Yip Yen at Hong Kong to use for the purpose.
He gave the picture a few days before he got the passport. When he arrived here he had some money, hut he did not remember how much.
With the view to finding out if witness re-fhembered seeing any of the men who came on the same boat, their photographs on the passports were shown to him. He was sick much of the time, he said, hut recollected seeing one out of the four men shown on the photographs.	.
Mr. Taylor left over his cross-examination until the morning, the judge, who said there had been difficulty in getting the man here, having it made clear that he must attend.
Yung Jung Sing, a very intelligent looking man. was put on the witness stand at five minutes to six o'clock.
He was a typesetter on the Sun Bow newspaper, Carrall Street, and had formerly worked for over three years for the ' Reform Ga-
He came from Hong Kong on the ' Mont-eagle,' hut not on the same trip as last witness. He was also a typesetter there and was not then, nor ever since, a merchant.
;So you see, this man admits he was not a merchant, but a typesetter. And these two typesetters say that they were allowed to enter the country without paying the poll
tax.
He got his passport-which had his photograph on it-from the Yah Wick Company of Devoe Road, Hong Kong.
That is one of the big companies handling these Chinese, trying to run them into the United States and Uanada.
This man Yip On was the official interpreter. He was sent to these men to train them and line them up to be passed. He passed them most successfully and in such a way that this government was defrauded out of one million dollars or more.
He gave him the gold on the steamer to put in his pocket in case he might be searched, so that he could hack up his story that he was a merchant, was about to go into business.
Yip On gave him some gold, which he put in his pocket, and then gave it hack to Yip On after he was examined.
Did he know if others on the boat did the same thing?-He looked only after his own business.
He was a wise Chinaman.
He was given just one letter by the Yah Wick Company at Hong Kong, to be handed to Yip On. Another man collected it from him on the voyage.
He knew nothing now as to whether the Yah Wick Company were still doing business.
I do not know either. I suppose that by this time there is no such company, for they would have had notice of that report.
Macdonald, collector of customs at Princo Rupert, was the first witness at the morning session.

He liad learned in Prince Rupert that Chinese were coming into Vancouver without paying the tax.
You will note that it was a well-known story all over the Coast for a long time before action was taken, that the Chinese were coming into Canada without paying poll tax and that this was virtually an open port so far as the Chinese were concerned.
Through the aid of the interpreter, afterwards getting permits and transmitting them to China for use by improper merchants, who would bring in with them boys described as sons, but who were not their sons. This state of matters had been going on for three years he was told by his informant, and the latter had come with him from Prince Rupert to give evidence.
There was a case in Toronto not many weeks ago. A bright, intelligent lad of 12 or 14 who was staying with a supposed uncle and who was brought to Toronto, no doubt as a merchant's son. The iad was found hanging dead in a room and was supposed to have committed suicide. But there is a great mystery about it. I contend that no Chinese boy should be admitted to this country except in company with his own parents. But this man knew and it was current report, that boys were admitted to Canada who pretended to be sons of men with whom they entered.
He had asked this man whether he had any proof to sustain the charges, but had been told that he knew it only by hearsay. In this it was mentioned that the price paid was $100 to the interpreter and $20 for others.
Cross-examined by Mr. S. S. Taylor witness said the name of his informant was Mar Ben Quin. Witness admitted he himself had no proof. He only mentioned what he had been told.
Mar Ben Quin, not having arrived, Yip On then got back to the witness stand, and was asked whether he had had anything to do in the way of inducing passengers to come over by the use of passports, or had he brought in mere working men as merchants?-No.
Did the Reform Association in 1907 by resolution ask him or Yip Suh Poy to bring over Chinese printers, and did not one of them cqme in under a passport?-No.
Asked again what he thought was the reason for his suspicion witness considered it was merely for the purpose of a government inspection. It was nothing to do with a tong war. He had heard on the street that Lew had made some trouble for him.
Mr. McCrossan switched back to the matter of passports and Dr. Chang, and the reason Dr. Chang had sent the list of names to witness instead of to Mr. Bowell, because a bone of contention between Mr. McCrossan and Mr. Taylor, the latter holding that Dr. Chang's letter, as coming from the Chinese diplomatic consul here, was absolutely free from any possibility of being impugned, and that he had kept that letter all through, as strong evidence in favour of his client.
Judge Murphy said that whether he had power to call Dr. Chang or not, he did not intend to do so.

After this little breeze was over Yip On was taken through another cable translating effort. This was a cable to ' Conclusion,' said to be Yip On's brother's code name, Hong Kong, and unsigned. It worked out roughly as follows:	' Suh Wy's position, suspended,
last boat, tell the people that know.' Mr. McCrossan assumed this to mean, on witnesses' explanation, that * Suh Wy's position,' meant ' little brother's position,' and contended that this cable was sent by Yip Quong, Yip On's brother. David Lew made the interpretation ' Suh Wy and his brother, position, suspended, last boat, tell everybody that knows.'
Reverting to the viceroy's certificate sent to Dr. Chang there was further argument between counsel and Judge Murphy stated that he believed it was a fact that every such certificate was duplicated at Ottawa. Mr. Taylor claimed that if this were the fact the passport conspiracy fell to the ground and protested further at the time taken up in bringing out matters in reference to Yip On, while other matters, such as the opium smuggling, were left over. The commission might go on for ever.
I would ask the Prime Minister if it is a fact that when Chinese entering Vancouver or Victoria in this way receive passports in China, duplicates of the passports are sent from the British consul in China direct to Ottawa as stated in this evidence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I could not tell my hon. friend at the moment?
Is there any minister hetre who could tell?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think there is?
Could the Minister of Inland Revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know.
Perhaps the Minister of Customs could tell? -
I could not state, but I suppose that if one was sent it would he sent to the Department of Trade and Commerce.

Perhaps the Minister of Militia, the latest recruit to the ranks of our diplomats, who has been practising the art lately with the intention of becoming High Commissioner,- could? Would he send a duplicate passport in this way? The Minister of Militia should be an expert on passports, as no one can enter his department without a passport. It would be a proper thing to have the photograph put on the passport. No one on the government benches knows anything about the Chinese question. But to resume the evidence.
Judge Murphy interposed. There are some people, he said, amidst general laughter, who say .that would be a good thing for us all. The opium matter was yet to come.	'

A good thing if the whole question was dropped. I wonder who the people were who the judge thought would like to see Ihe whole thing dropped.
Mar Ben Quin not having arrived, Yip On then got back into the witness stand and was asked whether he had had anything to do in the way of inducing passengers to come over by the use of passports, or had he brought in mere workingmen as merchants? No.
Did the Reform Association in 1907 by resolution ask him or Yip Su Foy to bring over Chinese printers and did not one of them come in under a passport. No.
Asked again what he thought was the reason for his suspension, witness considered it was merely for the purpose of a government inspection. It had nothing to do with -a Tong war
Yip On was then cross-examined by Mr. Gordon Grant concerning the method of examinations at the shed, and wanted to know if Mr. Bowell had refused permission to a man claiming to be a partner of Yip Sang, Yip On's partner. Witness did not notice if any of his uncle's partners had tried to come in.
Mr. Grant stated that Mr. Bowell had said that a man, so claiming, had tried to come
in and had been refused. Would witness say Mr. Bowell was wrong? Witness only said:	No.
He did not know how many partners his uncle had.
Why did he not know how many partners his uncle had? Because, perhaps, 200 Chinamen had each given $10 to become partners.
As regarded his brother, Yip Quong, he kept a jewellery store, starting three or four years ago, before which he was working in Wing San's. He had partners, of which witness was one, and Yip Quong and Yip Sam others, but he could not remember the names of others.
Three or four years ago he was Vice-President of the Reform Association.

Our duty as public men, involving as it does a party system imposes it upon us to observe gentlemanly rules of conduct. One of these gentlemanly rules is that no man on the floor of this House should be charged with any wrong doing or dishonesty or fraud unless the proof is in the hands of the man who prefers the charge. It is for that reason that I have hesitated to. use in a public way, either on the public platform or in this House, the material reported in the public press with reference to that investigation. I have hesitated to use it because I did not know how much of the evidence was reported correctly, how much of it was omitted, how much of it was distorted from its true meaning, and I regret, therefore, that the absolute refusal of the government to bring down to this House, and make known to the people of Canada- the real evidence, and the real report based upon that evidence compels us in the interest of the public, and in the interest of justice to deal with the evidence such as we have it in the reports of newspapers. We are inducing the people of the Orient to come to our shores, we are telling them that if they will come to Canada they need not have $50 in their pockets as the beastly British immigrant has to have, and while we do this why do we not attempt to elevate their mental and moral nature. They are the nroduct of a civilization older than ours; 2,000 years before Christ the Chinese empire had a civilization as developed as it is to-day, but it is a civilization that is not our civilization. If we induce these people to come to our shores, we should set them a good political and moral example and not teach them that when they reach Vancouver they can make a dicker with Mr. Party Heeler, living on Graft street by which they can discount their head tax of $500 by a large percentage and come in as merchant princes, instead of coolies and labourers. We should not let them see that the men who perpetrate these iniquities are not only allowed to go scot free, but are promoted to higher ofiice, are sent as trade commissioners to Japan or China, and are placed in positions of honour and power. The callousness with which the governments looks on at wrong-doing of this kind must have a bad effect upon the public life of Canada and more especially upon the orientals, for whom the Prime Minister has so much care. Now, I want to speak of another and a very important matter. On Friday, the 14th of July, 1911, there was consummated a new treaty of alliance between Great Britain and Japan, and which is of peculiar significance to the people of Canada, inasmuch as it removes the apprehension which existed under the treaty of 1905, and the preceding treaty of 1902, that in'case of trouble between Japan and the United States the mother land would be compelled by the terms of the treaty to take sides with Japan.
I am happy to say that this new treaty, entered into on Friday last, puts an eiid to the possibility of such a contingency ever happening. It provides' in express terms that in case of war between the
United States and Japan, the United Kingdom shall not be obliged to join on the side of Japan. That is a matter of rejoicing to the people of Canada, because we cannot forget that our good neighbours on the other side of the line are of the breed of our own sturdy race. For 2000 years we were of the same family; the common jurisprudence which they and we enjoy came down from Blackstone and Coke to Marshall and Story. Our common literature is enriched at times by a Tennyson, at times by ta Longfellow. The two countries have much in common. To each country our German friends have added their intelligence, their industry, their thrift, and our French people have added not only these, but their brilliancy and their love of art. So that they and we have much in common. But I think the Premier, when he was induced after much reluctance to put his seal of approval upon the little document which the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs brought back from Washington, wituout even crossing a 't' or dotting an 'i,' after it left the hand of President Taft, forgot the fact that although we and our good neighbours to the south have all these things? in common, yet we do not keep house together. We each must clean our own doorstep and warm ourselves at our own fireside, and I think it is good and well that it should be so, and as long as that is the case, I think our good Premier, whose brilliant gifts in other respects, I will say, have been an enrichment of our public life, should discuss public questions on their merits. But he failed to see the merits of the situation when he forgot that we and our good neighbours to the south do not keep house together; he forgot that each country must solve its own domestic problems according to its own point of view, and that as long as Canada remains a part of the British empire there is imposed. upon Canada the plain duty of having at least some regard for those interests which we have in common with the other parts of the empire when we seek to establish new relations with a foreign country. As to the application of this to the question in hand, I still have hope to pierce the thick veil of partisanship in some of our friends across the floor of this House, and reach the gray matter and influence the will and form the intelligence of those gentlemen. I still have hope to convince them that the cobweb robe with which they clothe themselves in regard to tuis Chinese inquiry, is indecent in the public eye, and exposes much that should not be exposed to the public eye of Canada. \s these great events are marching down the grooves of change in the political history of the world, Canada should be up and doing as a prime and foremost nation amongst the nations of the world. Cana-

da's duty is not to hold back, but to proceed with the other parts of the empire, and to strengthen the bond and to cast away that foolish fear that there may be found some one in some part of the empire thrusting at the rise of Canada and tearing away our autonomy. That figment of the imagination, fed to the minds of the people of Canada, will tend to mislead them, and it behoves the public men who can rise to the height of informing the electorate of Canada as to their real duty, instead of appealing to their fears, to assume the duty of protecting the destinies of Canada in the future.
If so, Canada will follow the course dictated by self-respect, nationhood and manhood, and that course will be that Canada will stand as a nation, and as the foremost in the great family of nations composing the British Empire.	_

You will have noticed that reference has been made several times during the debate to this clause by hon. gentlemen opposite. Looking at it from a purely business Mr. COWAN.
standpoint, I have been unable to find a single instance in which the preferential clause is of benefit to the farmers of Canada. Can any hon. gentleman in this House name one single article of Canadian product that gets a preference in the British market either in Canadian manufactures or in Canadian farm products. Canadian manufactures and Canadian farm products of all kinds sell in the British market on their merits, and that is the reason why the Americans are so anxious that the Reciprocity Bill should pass. They want to import Canadian farm products into the United States, and export them into Great Britain as American products. But, Mr. Speaker, while the American government is anxious to have reciprocity in farm products, they take very good care not to allow these products to enter their country after being partly manufactured. We know that while they will admit a million bushels of Canadian wheat into their country free of duty, the very moment you turn that million bushels irto flour they charge you a duty upon it. Why is it? Because the government of that country has always looked after the interests of the American workingman, and anv labour that has to be done on that million bushels of wheat they want done in the United States. Take the case of lumber, it is said that they will admit lumber into the United States free, in its rough state. That is true, but the moment you plane a board on one side, and export it to the United States there is a duty imposed upon it. Why? Because they are preserving that labour for the American workman, instead of having it done in Canada for the benefit of the Canadian workman.	.
I	cannot think for one moment that our farmers are going to stand for any such fraudulent bargain as this. They have the British market now, and they aTe going to 3o their best to keep it. It is a well known fact that the preferential clause means a larger importation of goods into this country, but what does that mean to the manufacturers of the country? What does it mean to the working class of the country? The greater part of every million dollars worth of manufactured goods that comes into this country might be manufactured here and supply labour and wages to the workmen of Canada.
Then, Mr. Speaker, you cannot but have noticed that there has been a frpe trade element in the speeches of some of the hon. gentlemen opposite in reference to the clause now under consideration. I regret that I have been obliged to speak at such length, but the question is a very important one. I am not presenting alone the case of the capitalists for whom I can assure you I have no retainer, but I feel that it is my duty as representing a large number of working men as near to the foot of the throne as I can, and as far as I am able to submit to the government and the people generally that some measures should be taken to enable these working ,men to have employment every day and to earn sufficient money to support' themselves and their families in comfort.
