It is not at all necessary for one to call himself a labour candidate or to sit in this House as a labour member in order that he should put those issues before this House. Representing as I do a large number of working people, although I do not pose as a labour candidate, I believe that it is my duty to the best of my ability to present to the country and to the House the interests of these people and to appeal for a remedy to the only institution in the land which had power to provide a remedy which will relieve us from any further imposition of this kind, and which will hold the markets of Canada for Canadian coal which we are capable of producing just as well as they can produce coal in a foreign country.

I do not imagine that my hon. friend desires to-night to challenge an opinion, and I would suggest therefore that the debate be adjourned so that at a later date when there is a better attendance of members any hon. member who desires may continue the discussion.
Now, that discussion was never coni tinued to my knowledge by the hon. member for North Cape Breton until this present session. It is utterly impossible to understand wihatt the hon. gentleman meant on that occasion when you compare the utterance that lie made then and his utterance during the present session of parliament. The coal industry of Nova Scotia has a capital invested in it of something in the vicinity of $1,000,000,000, it has 10,000 or 12,000, possibly more, men directly dependent upon it, and for us in Nova Scotia the coal question is a very important one indeed. Speaking as one representing the coal industry of Nova Scotia, while we would like to have seen .the duty remain as it was, and while we think it would have been perfectly justifiable to let it remain, we are content to take our share of the burden of taxation upon the people, and if eight cents a ton has been taken oft that coal we must put up with it, and do the best we can.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am expressing my own opinion. I do not object to my hon. friend having his opinion of what is in the public interest, but I think I am doing no wrong in expressing what I believe to be in the public interest. My hon. friend and I differ, that is our mutual misfortune.

It may be my hon. friend's misfortune,- I .do not regard it as mine. I was about to say that if matters of public importance are brought forward by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, such, for example, as the loss to the people of this country of a million dollars by a system of boodling, I ask if it be reasonable that we should be obliged to sit to an unreasonable hour simply because that particular matter has been brought to the attention of the House today. However, the hon. gentleman is entitled to his own opinion on the subject. I am certainly entitled to mine and the proposition, as I understand the hon. gentleman, is that no man on this side of the House shall be at liberty to bring to the attention of parliament, or the country any matter of any public interest whatever except at the risk of being obliged to sit to a very late hour in order to make up that time by a continuation of the reciprocity debate.
That is the proposition as I understand it. No matter what the subject may be- it may relate to the danger to the west of suffering from a coal famine, it may relate to irregularities and abuses in the public service-no one on this side of the House is to be at liberty to open his mouth in regard to any one of these subjects except under the penalty suggested by the hon. Minister of Finance. That may be regarded as a reasonable proposition; certainly, I desire to enter my protest against it at the earliest moment.

From the time the House met in November, for three or four months, there seemed to be an abundance of time. Members on the government side spoke for three or four hours, and there seemed to be very little objection. But things have taken a very sudden change to-night. The Minister of Finance suggests that the time is precious and that we should not take up the time of the House. It seems to me it is a policy of sit tight.
I have been looking for the time to come when we would hear from the ministers on the government side of the House what they were going to do for the people of Canada. We have heard them tell us that reciprocity was going to be a great thing for Canada-that it was	going to
enrich the farmer-going to do a lot for this country; but I have yet to find that they have ever made one tittle of proof that either nationally or financially we would be any further ahead than we are to-day. It puts me in mind of what happened last winter between two neighbours of mine-call them Jones and Smith. Jones had a very nice chesnut mare, and had been trying to get a mate for it. Smith was a professional horse trader, and he came along one evening about dark and said to Mr. FIELDING
Jones: 'I hear you have a nice chestnut mare. Now, I have a good mate for her. I will give you a trade for this horse.' Jones took him to be sincere, and asked him if the horse was all right, he said it was.,' adding ' If you take this horse it will go very well with yours, and you can do a lot of work with them, or if you want to sell the team you can make a pile of money out of them.' The trade was made, the next morning when Jones went to look at his matched team he found to his surprise that the new horse was broken winded, was heavy, had ringbones and was bogspavined. In fact everything that was bad. When he hitched them up and tried to drive off the new horse baulked and would not go at all. Now, I am of the opinion that many of the arguments put up here in connection with reciprocity are similar to this horse trade.
From the time the House adjourned on the 19th of May last up to the present time, I have had the pleasure of meeting the great majority of the electors of the county which I have the honour to represent, and, knowing what I am talking about, I should say that at least 90 or 95 per cent of the people of that county are absolutely opposed to reciprocity. When you consider that about 85 per cent of these people are farmers, why should we not say that they are thinking justly and rightly. Just think for one moment of the position of the farmers in the Dominion of Canada. They claim they have not got justice, and I claim they have not got justice. For instance, this present government will spend in one year between $140,000,000 and $150,000,000, and the farmers of Canada-who are the source of wealth, constituting 63 per cent of the population of this country will get less than $1,000,000, for there is less than $1,000,000 spent on agriculture. I say the farmers of this country have not been rightly used, and I say further that this government would be doing very much more for the farmers of Canada if they would help them financially in their agricultural pursuits.
If this reciprocity treaty goes into force the farmer of Canada will be in competition with the world without any protection whatever. After growing his wheat he takes it a mile down the road to the miller, and the moment it is turned into flour there is a duty on it. If he takes a load of hogs to the_ market^ he has to sell the hogs in competition with the world, but if he wants to take a pound of bacon home with him he has to pay duty. If he takes a steer or sheep to the market he has to sell it in competition with the world, but if he wants to take a pound of fresh meat with him he has to pay duty on it. I would ask the hon. members of this House if that is fair play for the farmer?

It is simply a matter of experiment with the farmer, who has been experimented with long enough, and I believe the day is not far distant when he will be experimented with no longer.
_ The farmers say to us: 'How is it that in 1900, 1904 and 1908, we never heard of reciprocity, yet it is thrown into the political arena now and we are told, here, take all or none.
The hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) made a statement here to the effect that he wanted the question discussed fairly and clearly, but on the very same column of 'Hansard' you will find that he gagged every member of the government and said that it must go through. He told them that the honour of the government and the honour of the House was pledged to this treaty. I would ask the hon. Finance Minister if the government was so particular about doing as the farmers of the Northwest asked, why is it that nothing was done for them? The hon, Finance Minister and the hon. Minister of Customs went to Washington and made a treaty with Mr. Taft and his legislators, which treaty they did not want to have broken. Seemingly they have no regard for the pledges made to the people of Canada, but they have respect for a pledge made with the American people or with the President of the United States-that is something which must not be broken.
We are asked who suggested this when it was brought before the people. I find that the hon. gentlemen on the government side tell us that previous to 1896 the Conservatives asked fox reciprocity. Well, I make the statement, and' I believe I am correct, that it is not on record in 'Hansard' that any Conservatives ever asked to make a treaty with the United States whereby the farmers would be divested of every vestige of protection and would, at the same time, have to pay duty for *every article they use. Why did the present government not do as the Conservative government did in 1893? in 1893, the Conservative government sent some of the cabinet ministers to many counties throughout this Dominion to find out the needs of the farmers. Amongst others- they came to the county which I have the honour to represent, and there were 20 farmers sent from different parts of that county t<o interview the cabinet ministers. These farmers were not Tories nor Grits, but Tories and Grits combined. It was- a representative deputation of farmers, and with the exception of one man, who asked for free corn, we stood solid, asking the government not to take the duty off farm produce, but rather to raise the duty on it. Now, if the farmers of the Dominion, and especially of Ontario, wanted the duty raised on farm produce in 1893, why should they want it taken off to-day? To-day we have trans-312}
portation facilities which we did not have then. We have spent almost $500,000,000 in building railways and canals, and to-day we have the British market nearer to us than the American mairket was at that time. No one will gainsay the fact that the British market to-day is far superior to- the American market which we had at that time.
We have heard it said that the farmers made a great deal of money previous to the McKinley Bill coming into force. This may be true. But as a farmer, I know- as well as any other man-that if we got high prices sometimes for our products, for years we did not get so much.
But what was that leading up to the deterioration of our farms. I can say as a farmer that, no matter where you went, especially in the province of Ontario, the soil was depleted of its fertility. The farms were not growing, in most cases, within five or ten bushels of grain per acre as much as they do to-day. Our coarse grain was sent to the United States, and with it our steers were sent out to be fattened on the American side. The McKinley Bill came into force and many farmers thought they were hurt. I was one of of those who were of that opinion. We had to look about us and see what we were going to do with our coarse grains, and especially with our barley. We went to work to raise stock, of which, previous to this, very little was raised in Ontario. We started to raise hogs and cattle. And as soon as we began on this course we had the fertility coming back on the land, and that is the reason we have the land in a superior state of fertility to what it was at that time. And I can honestly say as a farmer that there is not a man in Ontario who is feeding his coarse grain to stock, as he should do, who sells his barley for less than 75 cents a bushel, and some of it is as high as $1.25. And this has been the case for the last ten years. Then, we have been compelled to build up the reputation of our farm produce and live stock in England. It took years to do that. I can remember when in the agricultural societies and farmers' institutes the idea constantly expressed was that we should try to build up a fine type of bacon hog. That took fifteen years to accomplish. But today we have that type of hog and our bacon stands second to none in the English market. Shall we allow the American hog to come in so that the American bacon shall be mixed with ours? Shall we allow Canadian bacon to be sent to the United States to be mixed with lower grade American bacon and sent to the English market there to lower the standard of our product? We are told that if the American market is not satisfactory we can still send to the English market. But we know that the Minister of Agriculture himself has

been telling us to send our best quality of cured meat and grain to the English market. This we have done, and it is because of that that we have such a reputation in that market. I quite admit that, for a small percentage of our farm produce, those of No. 1 standard we should probably get a higher price in the United States. But, while we get a little more for twenty per cent of our farm produce we shall get far less for eighty per cent. If we sell this high quality cured meats and grain to the United States, we have only the lower grades to send to the English market. The result will be to lower our standard and our reputation and the reputation of our farm produce in England, so that it will take another fifteen or twenty years to regain what we have lost.
Now, we have been told that from 1854 to 1856 good times reigned in Canada because we had reciprocity. But times are different to-day from what they were then. Simply because the times were good then with reciprocity between Canada and the United States, is that any reason why we should expect prosperity now under reciprocity? We cannot judge of the future by the past. Our fathers lived in log houses, but we do not want to go back to houses of that kind. We have been progressing in the last fifteen or twenty years, and we want to still go on. But some people insist upon judging the future by the past. They would hark back to the days of 18541866 and say that because reciprocity was good for Canada then it must be good for Canada now. It is not necessarily so. I believe that it was a good thing then, but to assume that it will be a good thing now is to assume that the conditions now are the same as the conditions were then. But they are not, decidedly not. When a farmer is told of the high prices received for his products during the latter part of the time that that treaty was in force he should remember that peculiar circumstances existed then that do not exist now. The great civil war was wholly within this period. The prices of that time were enormous, and need not be expected to-day. Think of our condition as a country then. There was not even a confederation of the provinces. Now, the scattered fragments of those days have been brought together and made one great Dominion. Then there had been no combined systematic attempt to find a market for our goods. Apparently the United States was our only market. We had not learned of the possibilities about us. Now, the federated provinces have expended $427,000,000 on railways and canals to develop means of transportation; the provincial governments have spent $36,000,000, and the municipalities $18,000,000 in the same direction. Furthermore, the provincial and federal governments Mr. BEST.
have guaranteed bonds for Tailway construction in Canada to the amount of $127,000,000 more. We are proposing a further expenditure of $75,000,000 to $100,000,000 for the Transcontinental railway. All this expenditure is to develop internal trade between the east and west, and make us independent of the markets of the United States. At the time of the la=t reciprocity agreement we were in large measure dependent on the United States for our markets. But we are not dependent on them now. The mother country has replaced the United States in this respect. Improved transportation and cold storage have brought the British market nearer to us to-day than the market of the United States was in 1854. In 1910, Great Britain took of our animals and their products $42,000,000 out of a total of $54,000,000 which was exported, equal to 77 per cent. Of our agricultural products they took $71,000,000 worth out of a total of $91,000,000, equal to nearly 80 per cent. In the same year the United States took of the first 20 per cent, and of the second 9 per cent. The United States took last year of our agricultural products only 7 per cent more than she took forty-two years ago. These figures show conclusively the ability of the mother country to take all our products, and at good figures. They prove our independence of the United States market. Let us. disabuse our minds of the idea that because reciprocity was a good thing for the Canadians in 1854 we need it now, that because it was profitable under conditions existing then it would be profitable under the changed conditions of to-day. Circumstances alter cases. Before we consider the effect of the proposed arrangement-, we must consider three things concerning this reciprocity treaty. Mr. Speaker, I would ask for an adjournment.
